concepts.name: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
concepts.summary: Position is where an object is, velocity is how fast and which way it moves, and acceleration is how the velocity changes over time. To make motion look real you add a bit of acceleration to velocity each frame, then add velocity to position each frame.
key_points: Position, velocity, and acceleration each have separate x and y parts in a 2D game
Velocity changes position; acceleration changes velocity
You ADD acceleration to velocity and ADD velocity to position each frame
Without acceleration, motion starts and stops instantly and looks fake
concepts.example_code:
acceleration = .1
for i in range(100):
    car.v += acceleration   # change velocity a little each step
    car.x += velocity       # change position by the velocity

concepts.name: The Game Loop and Drawing a Frame
concepts.summary: A Pygame program runs a loop that handles events, updates positions, clears the screen, draws everything, and then shows the new frame. Clearing the screen each frame stops objects from leaving trails behind them.
key_points: The event loop (for event in pygame.event.get()) reads things like the close button
event.type == pygame.QUIT means the player clicked the window's X
screen.fill(color) clears the previous frame so nothing leaves a trail
pygame.display.flip() shows the newly drawn frame on screen
concepts.example_code:
for event in pygame.event.get():
    if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
        running = False
screen.fill(BACKGROUND_COLOR)
pygame.draw.rect(screen, SQUARE_COLOR, (x, y, SQUARE_SIZE, SQUARE_SIZE))
pygame.display.flip()
clock.tick(FPS)

concepts.name: Frame Rate and Delta Time
concepts.summary: Games redraw the screen many times a second. FPS is frames per second, and clock.tick(FPS) keeps the speed steady on every computer. The time step d_t = 1/FPS is multiplied into motion so things move the same real-world speed no matter the frame rate.
key_points: clock = pygame.time.Clock() and clock.tick(FPS) cap the frame rate
d_t = 1 / FPS is how long one frame lasts
Multiplying speed by d_t keeps motion consistent across computers
concepts.example_code:
FPS = 60
d_t = 1 / FPS  # Time step for physics calculations
...
x = x + d_x
clock.tick(FPS)

concepts.name: Reading Keyboard Input
concepts.summary: pygame.key.get_pressed() returns an array telling you which keys are held down right now. You check entries like keys[pygame.K_LEFT] to decide how to move the player.
key_points: keys = pygame.key.get_pressed() gives the state of every key
Constants like pygame.K_LEFT, pygame.K_RIGHT, pygame.K_SPACE name keys
Holding a key keeps moving the object while it is pressed

concepts.name: Edge Collisions and Bouncing
concepts.summary: A simple collision is hitting the edge of the screen. You detect it when a position goes past the screen size or below zero, and you make the object bounce by reversing (negating) its velocity in that direction.
key_points: Detect an edge collision when x or y passes the screen size or goes below 0
Bounce by reversing the velocity in the colliding direction
Reversing only the colliding direction's velocity gives a realistic bounce

concepts.name: Gravity and Jumping
concepts.summary: Gravity is a downward acceleration added to the y velocity every frame. Because the top of the screen is y=0, moving up means a negative y velocity. A jump sets a negative y velocity, then gravity slows the rise, stops it, and pulls the object back down.
key_points: On screen y=0 is the top, so up is a NEGATIVE y velocity
Gravity is added to velocity_y each frame: velocity_y += gravity * d_t
A jump sets velocity_y to a negative starting value
Landing on the ground stops the fall by setting velocity to 0
concepts.example_code:
velocity_y = -settings.jump_velocity_y     # jump upward
...
velocity_y += settings.gravity * settings.d_t  # gravity pulls down
y_pos += velocity_y * settings.d_t

questions.question: In a Pygame physics program, what does acceleration directly change?
questions.answer: The velocity
questions.explanation: Acceleration is added to velocity each frame, and velocity then changes position.

questions.question: Why do we add a little acceleration to velocity each frame instead of setting velocity to full speed all at once?
questions.answer: So the object speeds up or slows down gradually, which makes the motion look realistic.
questions.explanation: Smoothly changing velocity each frame avoids unrealistic instant starts and stops.

questions.question: What kind of motion does this code produce for the red square?
questions.code:
a = (-K * (x_pos - center)) / mass
velocity += a * d_t
x_pos += velocity * d_t
options: It moves at a constant speed forever
It oscillates back and forth around the center like it is attached to a spring
questions.answer: It oscillates back and forth around the center like it is attached to a spring
questions.explanation: The acceleration always points back toward the center, producing spring-like oscillation.

questions.question: All of an object's motion in these 2D games can be described by movement in which two directions?
questions.answer: The x direction (left and right) and the y direction (up and down).
questions.explanation: 2D games split motion into independent x and y components.

questions.question: If FPS = 60, what is the value of d_t = 1 / FPS?
questions.answer: About 0.0167 (which is 1/60)
questions.explanation: d_t is the fraction of a second each frame takes: 1 divided by frames per second.

questions.question: What is the purpose of clock.tick(FPS) at the end of the game loop?
options: It caps the frame rate so the game runs at a consistent speed on all computers
questions.answer: It caps the frame rate so the game runs at a consistent speed on all computers
questions.explanation: tick(FPS) limits how many frames run per second.

questions.question: Which Pygame function returns an array of all keys and whether each one is currently pressed?
questions.answer: pygame.key.get_pressed()
questions.explanation: You read it with constants like keys[pygame.K_LEFT].

questions.question: Which key, when held, moves the square to the right in this code?
questions.answer: pygame.K_RIGHT
questions.explanation: K_RIGHT sets a positive d_x, moving the square right.

questions.question: Because the top of the screen is y=0, what velocity makes an object move UP?
questions.answer: A negative y velocity
questions.explanation: Up is toward y=0, so decreasing y (negative velocity) moves the object up.

questions.question: Which line correctly applies gravity each frame so the object falls faster over time?
questions.answer: velocity_y += gravity * d_t
questions.explanation: Gravity is an acceleration added to the y velocity every frame.

questions.question: To make a ball bounce off the left or right wall of the screen, what do you do to its x velocity?
questions.answer: Reverse (negate) it, for example velocity_x = -velocity_x.
questions.explanation: Negating the velocity sends the object back in the opposite direction.

questions.question: Which condition detects that the square has hit the bottom (the ground)?
questions.answer: y_pos + square_size > screen_height
questions.explanation: The bottom edge of the square passing screen_height means it reached the ground.

questions.question: What does pygame.display.flip() do in the game loop?
options: It flips the player upside down
It shows the newly drawn frame on the screen
questions.answer: It shows the newly drawn frame on the screen
questions.explanation: flip() swaps the freshly drawn surface in so the player sees the new frame.

questions.question: Why is screen.fill(BACKGROUND_COLOR) called at the start of every frame?
options: To clear the previous frame so the moving square does not leave a trail
questions.answer: To clear the previous frame so the moving square does not leave a trail
questions.explanation: Filling the screen erases the old drawing before the new one.

questions.question: Which event type tells the program that the player clicked the window's close button?
questions.answer: pygame.QUIT
questions.explanation: Checking event.type == pygame.QUIT lets the loop stop running.

concepts.name: Classes and Objects
concepts.summary: A class is a blueprint (a new data type) and an object is one thing built from that blueprint. Every object has identity (its name), state (its variables/attributes), and behavior (its functions/methods). You use the dot (.) to reach an object's parts.
key_points: A class is a blueprint/datatype; an object is an instance made from it
Objects have identity (name), state (attributes), and behavior (methods)
The dot (.) accesses an object's attributes and methods
Pygame is designed to be object-oriented

concepts.name: The __init__ Method and self
concepts.summary: __init__ is the initializer that runs automatically when an object is created; it sets up the object's starting attributes. The first parameter, self, refers to the specific object being worked on, and self.name = name stores data inside that object.
key_points: __init__ runs automatically when an object is created
self refers to the particular object the method is acting on
self.attribute = value stores state inside the object

concepts.name: Inheritance and super()
concepts.summary: Inheritance lets a new (derived) class reuse an existing (base) class and then add or change behavior. A derived class is a 'kind of' the base class. super() calls the parent class's version of a method.
key_points: class Parent(Person): means Parent inherits from Person
A derived class is a 'kind of' its base class
super().__init__(...) calls the parent's initializer
The derived class gets all the parent's attributes and methods plus its own

concepts.name: Polymorphism
concepts.summary: Polymorphism means 'many forms': the same method name can do different things in different classes, and any function written for a base class also works on its derived classes. So a function for a Person also works on a Parent or a Child.
key_points: The same method name can behave differently in different classes
A function for a base class also accepts objects of its derived classes
Overriding a method in a child gives it different behavior than the parent
concepts.example_code:
def get_name_and_age(person: Person):
    print(f"{person.name} is {person.age} years old.")

get_name_and_age(mom)      # a Parent
get_name_and_age(charlie)  # a Child

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between a class and an object?
options: A class is a copy of an object
A class is a blueprint and an object is built from it
An object is a blueprint for a class
They are exactly the same thing
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint and an object is built from it
questions.explanation: A class defines the type; an object is one instance made from that blueprint.

questions.question: Name the three things every object has, according to the lesson.
questions.answer: Identity, state (attributes), and behavior (methods).
questions.explanation: These three together define what an object is in OOP.

questions.question: Given the Person class, which line creates a Person object named Alice who is 14?
questions.answer: alice = Person("Alice", 14)
questions.explanation: Calling the class like a function runs __init__ and builds the object.

questions.question: Which symbol do you use to access an object's attribute or method, like getting alice's name?
questions.answer: The dot (.)
questions.explanation: alice.name uses the dot to reach the name attribute inside the object.

questions.question: When does the __init__ method run?
options: Automatically when a new object is created
Only when you call it by name
questions.answer: Automatically when a new object is created
questions.explanation: __init__ is the initializer that runs as the object is built.

questions.question: Inside a method, what does the parameter self refer to?
questions.answer: The specific object the method is being called on.
questions.explanation: self lets a method read and change that object's own attributes.

questions.question: What does the line self.name = name do inside __init__?
questions.answer: It stores the name value as an attribute (state) on the object being created.
questions.explanation: It saves data inside the object so it can be used later.

questions.question: What will this code print?
questions.answer: Alice
questions.explanation: alice.name returns the value stored when the object was created.

questions.question: What does the line class Parent(Person): mean?
questions.answer: Parent inherits from Person
questions.explanation: Putting Person in the parentheses makes Parent a derived class of Person.

questions.question: What does super().__init__(name, age) do inside a derived class's __init__?
questions.answer: It calls the parent class's initializer to set up the inherited attributes.
questions.explanation: super() reuses the parent's setup code instead of rewriting it.

questions.question: Even though the Parent class never defines its own name or age variable, why can a Parent object still use say_hello?
options: Because say_hello is a built-in Python function
Because it is inherited from the Person class
Because Parent is a copy of say_hello
questions.answer: Because it is inherited from the Person class
questions.explanation: A derived class inherits the attributes and methods of its base class.

questions.question: What does polymorphism mean?
options: A class can have many objects
The same method name can do different things in different classes
A program can have many classes
questions.answer: The same method name can do different things in different classes
questions.explanation: 'Poly' means many and 'morph' means form, so the method takes many forms.

questions.question: The function get_name_and_age(person) was written for a Person. Why can you also pass it a Parent or a Child object?
options: Because Parent and Child are kinds of Person (polymorphism)
Because all functions accept any object
Because Parent and Child have no __init__
questions.answer: Because Parent and Child are kinds of Person (polymorphism)
questions.explanation: Derived classes can be used anywhere their base class is expected.

questions.question: In the code tina = Turtle() and tina.forward(150), name the class, the object, and the method.
questions.answer: Class: Turtle; object: tina; method: forward().
questions.explanation: Turtle is the blueprint, tina is the instance, forward() is its behavior.

concepts.name: What a Vector Is
concepts.summary: A vector combines an x and a y value into one object. You can think of it as a point (x, y) in space, or as a line with a length (magnitude) and a direction (angle). A plain single number, like 8, is called a scalar.
key_points: A 2D vector holds an x value and a y value together
It can be seen as a point OR as a direction-and-magnitude
magnitude is the length: sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
A regular single number is called a scalar

concepts.name: Vector Math: Scaling and Adding
concepts.summary: Two key operations: multiplying a vector by a scalar (scaling) makes it longer or shorter without changing direction, and adding two vectors adds their x parts together and their y parts together.
key_points: vector * scalar multiplies both x and y by the scalar (scaling)
vector + vector adds the x's together and the y's together
Scaling changes length but not direction
Adding a movement vector to a position vector moves the object
concepts.example_code:
v1 = Vector2(10, 10)
v2 = Vector2(20, 20)
print(v1 + v2)  # Vector2(30, 30)

concepts.name: Pygame's Vector2
concepts.summary: Instead of writing your own vector class, games use pygame.math.Vector2, which has many built-in features. You store positions and velocities as Vector2 objects and update them with simple addition like p1 += move.
key_points: from pygame.math import Vector2 imports the class
Vector2(100, 100) makes a vector at x=100, y=100
p1 += move is the same as p1 = p1 + move
Using vectors keeps position/velocity code shorter and clearer
concepts.example_code:
p1 = Vector2(100, 100)
move = Vector2(10, 0)  # 10 pixels right
p1 += move  # p1 is now (110, 100)

concepts.name: Rotating Vectors
concepts.summary: Because a vector has a direction, you can rotate it. rotate_ip(angle) rotates the vector in place (changes it), while rotate(angle) returns a new rotated vector. Rotation is how you point movement or thrust in any direction.
key_points: rotate_ip(angle) rotates the vector in place (modifies it)
rotate(angle) returns a NEW rotated vector instead
The _ip suffix means 'in place'
An easy way to aim a vector: make it the right length pointing right, then rotate it
concepts.example_code:
move = Vector2(100, 0)  # 100-unit vector pointing right
move.rotate_ip(45)      # rotate to 45 degrees in place
p1 += move

questions.question: What does a 2D vector contain?
options: An x value and a y value
questions.answer: An x value and a y value
questions.explanation: A 2D vector groups an x and a y together into one object.

questions.question: What is the special word for a plain single number (like 8), as opposed to a vector?
questions.answer: A scalar.
questions.explanation: Multiplying a vector by a scalar scales its length.

questions.question: The lesson says a vector can be thought of in two equal ways. Which pair is correct?
options: A point in space, or a direction and magnitude
A speed and a frame rate
questions.answer: A point in space, or a direction and magnitude
questions.explanation: A point (x,y) and a line with length and direction from the origin describe the same vector.

questions.question: What is the formula for the magnitude (length) of a vector with components x and y?
questions.answer: sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
questions.explanation: Magnitude is the Pythagorean distance of the vector from the origin.

questions.question: What does Vector2(10, 10) + Vector2(20, 20) equal?
questions.answer: Vector2(30, 30)
questions.explanation: Adding vectors adds the x parts and the y parts: 10+20 and 10+20.

questions.question: Multiplying a vector by a scalar (scaling) does what?
options: Makes it longer or shorter without changing direction
Turns it into a single number
questions.answer: Makes it longer or shorter without changing direction
questions.explanation: Scaling changes magnitude (length) but keeps the same direction.

questions.question: Using the rules from the lesson, what is the vector (2, 3) multiplied by the scalar 5?
questions.explanation: Scaling multiplies each component by the scalar: 2*5 and 3*5.

questions.question: Which line correctly imports Pygame's built-in vector class?
questions.answer: from pygame.math import Vector2
questions.explanation: Vector2 lives in pygame.math (you can also do from pygame import Vector2).

questions.question: After this code runs, what is p1?
questions.code:
p1 = Vector2(100, 100)
move = Vector2(10, 0)
p1 += move
questions.explanation: Adding move adds 10 to x and 0 to y.

questions.question: To move a player by a movement vector, what do you do with that vector and the player's position vector?
options: Add the movement vector to the position vector
Subtract the position from the movement
Rotate the position by the movement
questions.answer: Add the movement vector to the position vector
questions.explanation: p1 += move moves the player by the movement vector.

questions.question: What is the difference between vector.rotate(45) and vector.rotate_ip(45)?
questions.answer: rotate(45) returns a new rotated vector; rotate_ip(45) rotates the vector in place, changing the original.
questions.explanation: The _ip suffix means 'in place'.

questions.question: In a Pygame vector method name, what does the _ip suffix stand for?
questions.answer: In place
questions.explanation: _ip methods modify the existing vector instead of returning a new one.

questions.question: What is an easy way to make a vector that points 45 degrees and is 100 units long?
options: Make a vector (100, 0) pointing right, then rotate it 45 degrees
questions.answer: Make a vector (100, 0) pointing right, then rotate it 45 degrees
questions.explanation: Build the length pointing right, then rotate to the angle you want.

questions.question: When the direction of a vector is 90 degrees (straight up or down), what is its X component?
questions.answer: Zero (the whole magnitude is in the Y component).
questions.explanation: At 90 degrees the vector has no left-right part, so X is 0.

concepts.name: Sprites: image and rect
concepts.summary: A sprite is a 2D image that represents a game object. In Pygame you make a sprite class by subclassing pygame.sprite.Sprite. Two attributes are special: image (what it looks like) and rect (a rectangle giving its position and size).
key_points: A sprite is a 2D image that represents a game object
Your sprite class subclasses pygame.sprite.Sprite
The image attribute is the surface drawn on screen
The rect attribute holds the sprite's position and size

concepts.name: Sprite Groups
concepts.summary: A sprite Group is a collection of sprites you can update and draw all at once. You add sprites with group.add(sprite); then group.update() calls every sprite's update(), and group.draw(screen) draws them all.
key_points: all_sprites = pygame.sprite.Group() creates a group
group.update() calls update() on every sprite in it
group.draw(screen) draws every sprite using its image and rect
With groups you don't write a separate draw() for each sprite in the main loop

concepts.name: Loading and Overriding Sprite Images
concepts.summary: You can load an image file with pygame.image.load() to give a sprite a real picture instead of a drawn shape. By subclassing and overriding the method that creates the image, a new class reuses everything else but shows a different picture.
key_points: pygame.image.load(path) loads an image file as a surface
Path(__file__).parent / 'images' finds the assets folder next to the file
Overriding create_spaceship_image() in a subclass swaps the picture
The subclass inherits all other behavior from the parent sprite class

concepts.name: Removing Sprites with kill()
concepts.summary: kill() is a Sprite method that removes a sprite from every group it belongs to, so it stops being updated and drawn. It is used for things like projectiles that fly off the screen and should disappear.
key_points: self.kill() removes a sprite from all its groups
A killed sprite is no longer updated or drawn
Useful for projectiles or objects that leave the screen
concepts.example_code:
# In a Projectile sprite, when it leaves the screen:
self.kill()  # remove from all groups

questions.question: What is a sprite in Pygame?
options: A 2D image that represents a game object
questions.answer: A 2D image that represents a game object
questions.explanation: Sprites are the images that move around the screen.

questions.question: What are the two special attributes a Pygame sprite uses?
questions.answer: image and rect
questions.explanation: image is what the sprite looks like; rect holds its position and size.

questions.question: What class should your own sprite class inherit from?
questions.answer: pygame.sprite.Sprite
questions.explanation: Subclassing pygame.sprite.Sprite gives your class the image/rect/group behavior.

questions.question: What does a sprite's rect attribute represent?
questions.answer: The rectangle that defines the sprite's position and size.
questions.explanation: The rect is how Pygame knows where and how big the sprite is.

questions.question: Which line creates a rect centered on a given position?
questions.answer: self.rect = self.image.get_rect(center=position)
questions.explanation: get_rect(center=position) builds a rect placed at that center point.

questions.question: How do you create an empty sprite group in Pygame?
questions.answer: pygame.sprite.Group()
questions.explanation: A Group collects sprites so you can update and draw them together.

questions.question: When you call all_sprites.update(), what happens?
options: The update() method of every sprite in the group is called
questions.answer: The update() method of every sprite in the group is called
questions.explanation: A group updates all of its sprites at once.

questions.question: In the sprite version of the game, why is there no separate draw() call for the spaceship and projectiles in the Game class?
options: The sprite group's draw() draws all of them at once
draw() is automatic on every Python object
questions.answer: The sprite group's draw() draws all of them at once
questions.explanation: all_sprites.draw(screen) handles drawing every sprite in the group.

questions.question: Which Pygame function loads an image file to use as a sprite's picture?
questions.answer: pygame.image.load()
questions.explanation: It returns a surface you can store in the sprite's image attribute.

questions.question: What does Path(__file__).parent / 'images' do?
options: Builds the path to the images folder next to the current file
questions.answer: Builds the path to the images folder next to the current file
questions.explanation: It locates the assets folder in the same directory as the running file.

questions.question: The AlienSpaceship subclass only overrides create_spaceship_image(). What is the result?
options: It keeps all Spaceship behavior but shows the alien image instead of the triangle
It makes the ship stop moving
questions.answer: It keeps all Spaceship behavior but shows the alien image instead of the triangle
questions.explanation: Overriding one method changes only the picture; everything else is inherited.

questions.question: What does the sprite method kill() do?
questions.answer: It removes the sprite from all groups, so it is no longer updated or drawn.
questions.explanation: kill() takes the sprite out of every group it belongs to.

questions.question: When should you call kill() on a projectile sprite?
options: At the start of the game
When it goes off the screen
When the player presses a key
questions.answer: When it goes off the screen
questions.explanation: Projectiles that leave the screen should disappear instead of wrapping around.

concepts.name: Types of Collision Detection
concepts.summary: Collisions detect when game objects touch. The three kinds are bounding box (rectangles around objects), circle (overlapping circles), and pixel-perfect (checking individual pixels). Bounding box and circle are fast but less accurate; pixel-perfect is the most accurate but the slowest.
key_points: Bounding box uses rectangles and is the simplest and most common
Circle collisions use overlapping circles
Pixel-perfect checks individual pixels — most accurate, slowest
A bounding box can report a collision before the visible images actually touch
concepts.example_code:
# Three collision types: bounding box, circle, pixel perfect.
# Bounding boxes are fast but can overlap before the images touch.

concepts.name: Detecting Collisions with spritecollide
concepts.summary: pygame.sprite.spritecollide() checks one sprite against a whole group of sprites and returns a list of the ones it is touching. If the list isn't empty, a collision happened, and you can react.
key_points: spritecollide(player, obstacles, dokill=False) checks a sprite vs a group
It returns a list of the sprites that collided (empty if none)
An empty list is falsy, so 'if collider:' tests for a collision
The dokill argument controls whether collided sprites are auto-removed

concepts.name: Rect Edges and Moving Rects
concepts.summary: A Rect has not just .x and .y but also .left, .right, .top, and .bottom for its edges, which you can read or write. You move a rect with .move (which returns a new rect) or .move_ip (which changes it in place).
key_points: Rect edges: .left, .right, .top, .bottom (readable and writable)
screen.get_rect() gives the screen's rectangle for off-screen checks
.move(dx, dy) returns a NEW rect; you must assign the result
.move_ip(dx, dy) moves the rect in place (changes the original)

questions.question: What are the three types of collision detection described in the lesson?
options: Bounding box, circle, and pixel perfect
questions.answer: Bounding box, circle, and pixel perfect
questions.explanation: These are the three approaches the lesson lists.

questions.question: Which collision type is the most accurate but also the slowest?
questions.answer: Pixel perfect
questions.explanation: Pixel-perfect checks individual pixels, so it is precise but slow.

questions.question: Which collision type does the lesson call the simplest, so it teaches it first?
questions.answer: Bounding box
questions.explanation: Bounding box collisions are fast and easy, so they are learned first.

questions.question: Why can a bounding box collision feel wrong to a player?
questions.answer: The rectangles can overlap (counting as a collision) even when the visible images aren't actually touching.
questions.explanation: Bounding boxes surround the image, so they can overlap before the art does.

questions.question: What does pygame.sprite.spritecollide(player, obstacles, dokill=False) return?
options: A list of the sprites in the group that collided with the player
questions.answer: A list of the sprites in the group that collided with the player
questions.explanation: An empty list means no collision; a non-empty list means a hit.

questions.question: What does this code do when the player touches an obstacle?
options: Explodes the first obstacle the player collided with
questions.answer: Explodes the first obstacle the player collided with
questions.explanation: collider[0] is the first sprite in the returned collision list.

questions.question: Why does 'if collider:' work as a test for whether a collision happened?
options: An empty list counts as False and a non-empty list counts as True
questions.answer: An empty list counts as False and a non-empty list counts as True
questions.explanation: If any sprites collided, the list is non-empty and the if block runs.

questions.question: What does the dokill argument to spritecollide control?
questions.answer: Whether the collided sprites are automatically removed from their groups.
questions.explanation: dokill=True kills the colliding sprites; dokill=False leaves them.

questions.question: What is the difference between rect.move(1, 0) and rect.move_ip(1, 0)?
options: move returns a new rect; move_ip changes the rect in place
questions.answer: move returns a new rect; move_ip changes the rect in place
questions.explanation: _ip means 'in place', so move_ip modifies the original rect.

questions.question: Besides .x and .y, name two edge attributes a Rect has.
questions.answer: Any two of: .left, .right, .top, .bottom.
questions.explanation: These give the coordinates of the rectangle's edges and can be read or set.

questions.question: How do you get a Rect representing the whole screen so you can check if a sprite went off it?
questions.answer: screen.get_rect()
questions.explanation: It returns the screen's rectangle, useful for comparing with sprite edges.

questions.question: What does player.rect.move_ip(1, 0) do?
options: Moves the rect 1 pixel to the right, changing it directly
Returns a new rect 1 pixel up
Moves the rect 1 pixel down without changing it
questions.answer: Moves the rect 1 pixel to the right, changing it directly
questions.explanation: move_ip changes the rect in place by the given x and y amounts.

concepts.name: Surfaces and blit
concepts.summary: A surface is anything you can draw on — like a blank sheet of paper. The screen, the background, and any loaded image are all surfaces. The key surface method is blit(), which copies one surface onto another.
key_points: A surface is anything you can draw on; the screen is the special display surface
Images loaded with pygame.image.load() and rendered text are also surfaces
blit() copies one surface onto another at a position
All surfaces share methods because they are all the same Surface class (polymorphism)
concepts.example_code:
image = pygame.Surface((screen.get_width(), screen.get_height()))
image.blit(bg_tile, (x, 0))  # copy bg_tile onto image at x

concepts.name: Tiling and Scrolling Backgrounds
concepts.summary: To fill a screen with a small background image, you tile it by blitting it repeatedly across the width using range(start, stop, step). To make a scrolling background, you draw it onto an image twice the screen width and move it left a pixel each frame, resetting when it scrolls off.
key_points: Tile by blitting an image at each x with range(0, screen_width, tile_width)
range(start, stop, step) generates the x positions
Scrolling uses an image 2x the screen width with the background drawn twice
Move the scrolling image left each frame and reset it when it is off screen
concepts.example_code:
for x in range(0, screen.get_width(), background_width):
    image.blit(bg_tile, (x, 0))

concepts.name: Spritesheets
concepts.summary: A spritesheet packs many small images into one big image so they are easy to manage. The SpriteSheet class loads the sheet and extracts a single sprite by index, or a strip of several. You tell it the cell size (like 16x16) when you create it.
key_points: A spritesheet holds many sprites in one image to keep them organized
SpriteSheet(path, (16, 16)) sets the size of each cell
image_at(index) loads one sprite; load_strip(start, count) loads several
colorkey=-1 uses the top-left pixel's color as transparent
concepts.example_code:
spritesheet = SpriteSheet(path, (16, 16))
sprite = spritesheet.image_at(0)
sprite_strip = spritesheet.load_strip(1, 3, colorkey=-1)

concepts.name: Frame-Based Animation
concepts.summary: To animate a character you load a list of images (one per pose) and switch which one is shown every few frames. Counting frames and using the modulo operator (%) advances to the next image at a steady pace and loops back to the start.
key_points: Load a list/strip of images, one per animation frame
frame_count % frames_per_image == 0 triggers a change every few frames
index = (index + 1) % len(sprites) loops through frames and wraps around
More frames per image means slower animation
concepts.example_code:
frame_count += 1
if frame_count % frames_per_image == 0:
    frog_index = (frog_index + 1) % len(frog_sprites)
screen.blit(frog_sprites[frog_index], (100, 100))

concepts.name: Image Transforms
concepts.summary: The pygame.transform module changes images: scale() resizes, rotate() spins by an angle, and flip() mirrors them. These let you do effects like rotating a moving ball or squashing a character when it lands.
key_points: pygame.transform.scale(image, (w, h)) resizes an image
pygame.transform.rotate(image, angle) rotates by an angle
pygame.transform.flip mirrors an image horizontally or vertically
Transforms create effects like spinning or stretching sprites
concepts.example_code:
image = pygame.transform.scale(image, (width, height))
image = pygame.transform.rotate(image, angle)

questions.question: What is the main trick for making a side-scrolling background?
questions.answer: Make an image twice the screen width, blit the background onto it twice, move it left one pixel each frame, and reset it when it goes off screen.

questions.question: Why do games use a spritesheet?

To pack many small images into one image so they are easier to manage

questions.question: To make an animation play more slowly, do you increase or decrease frames_per_image?
